lesson.title: No Single Point of Failure: Building Defense in Depth
lesson.summary: Defense in depth arranges multiple, independent layers of security controls so that the failure of any one layer does not by itself hand an attacker the whole prize.
lesson.body:
Defense in depth is the practice of layering security controls so that no single control, if it fails or is bypassed, is enough on its own to compromise the system. The idea borrows its name from military strategy, where an attacker who breaks through one line of defense still has to fight through the next one, and the one after that, rather than winning outright at the first breach.

The previous two chapters make the motivation for this concrete. ARP spoofing showed that trust built into the local link layer can be broken by anyone already on the network. DNS cache poisoning showed that trust in a shared resolver can be broken by an attacker who is not even on the same network. In both cases, a single mechanism that everything else quietly depended on turned out to be exploitable. A network that relies on just one control, say, a firewall at the perimeter, has nothing left protecting it once that one control is bypassed or misconfigured, whether the bypass comes from an insider, a compromised device, or one of the spoofing techniques already covered.

Defense in depth answers this by stacking independent layers, each covering for the others' potential failure. A typical layered setup might include a perimeter firewall, internal network segmentation that limits how far an attacker can move after breaching one host, encrypted transport protecting the confidentiality of data even in transit, host level protections like promptly patched software, and monitoring and logging that can detect unusual activity even when prevention fails. The ARP spoofing scenario from earlier is a good test case: if an attacker successfully forges ARP replies and positions themselves as a man in the middle on the local network, that is a failure of the link layer's implicit trust. But if the traffic flowing through that connection is encrypted, the attacker captures only unreadable ciphertext. One layer failed, but the layer underneath it still held, and the data itself was protected.

Notice that these layers serve different purposes beyond just blocking an attacker outright. Some layers are meant for prevention, some for detection, and some for limiting how much damage a successful breach can do. A compromise at any single layer should ideally still trigger an alert somewhere else in the stack, or at minimum keep the damage contained to a small part of the network rather than spreading everywhere, which is exactly the opposite of a network that trusted one perimeter control to do all the work.
